title: What is a 1099-MISC Form? What it reports and who gets one
summary: What is a 1099-MISC form? See the income it reports, who receives one, how it differs from the 1099-NEC, and how to handle it. Read on.
body_markdown:
If a form marked "1099-MISC” has landed in your inbox, or you need to send one, then you’ve found the perfect article that explains all you need to know. I explain what the 1099-MISC form reports, who gets one, how it differs from the 1099-NEC, and what to do with it.


The 1099-MISC is one of the IRS 1099 forms, and it has changed significantly in recent years. It reports miscellaneous income such as rent, prizes, awards, and certain legal settlements. Since 2020, contractor and freelance pay has been reported on the separate 1099-NEC form, so the 1099-MISC now covers other income categories. The payer sends it to the recipient and the IRS.


## What is a 1099-MISC form?


A 1099-MISC form is an IRS information return that reports certain payments that are not wages and, since 2020, are not contractor pay. The IRS describes it as the form used to report rents, royalties, prizes and awards, and other fixed or determinable income.


It works like this. A business or other payer that paid you money during the year files the form with the IRS, so the IRS knows what you received. The payer also sends you a copy, so you can report the income on your own tax return. The form is not a bill, and it doesn’t say you owe tax. It’s a record of what was paid.


The 1099-MISC used to be the all-purpose 1099. Before 2020, freelancer and contractor pay was reported in one of its boxes. From 2020, that pay moved to a separate form, the 1099-NEC, which stands for nonemployee compensation. That change left the 1099-MISC for everything else, which is why people who still call every contractor form a “1099-MISC” are using an older name.


The 1099-MISC is one of several 1099 forms. For a wider look at the family, see our guide to[what a 1099 form is](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099) .


## What the 1099-MISC reports


The 1099-MISC reports rents, royalties, prizes and awards, and a handful of other payment types. Each category has its own box on the form, as shown in the table below. The box numbers follow the current IRS instructions for 2026 forms.


Box What it reports Typical examples


1 Rents Rent a business pays for office space, equipment, or other property


2 Royalties Payments for the use of intellectual property or natural resources


3 Other income Prizes, awards, damages, and other taxable payments that fit no other box


4 Federal income tax withheld Backup withholding, when a payee has not provided a taxpayer ID


6 Medical and health care payments Payments to doctors and other health care providers for services


8 Substitute payments in lieu of dividends or interest Payments a broker makes in place of dividends or tax-exempt interest


9 Crop insurance proceeds Payments from crop insurance


10 Gross proceeds paid to an attorney Payments to a lawyer in connection with legal services, such as a settlement paid through them


There are also a few less common items, such as direct sales of consumer products for resale and certain deferred compensation payments. The[IRS instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099mec) list every box.


Two things you should note:


- **Settlements:** A legal settlement is reported in different boxes depending on what it covers. Damages can fall under other income, while money paid to a lawyer is reported as gross proceeds paid to an attorney.
- **Backup withholding:** If a payer withholds federal tax because you didn’t provide a taxpayer ID, it is reported in box 4, whatever the amount.


## Who gets a 1099-MISC?


You get a 1099-MISC if a payer paid you at least the reporting threshold in one of the covered categories during the year. The threshold depends on the type of payment, and many of them have changed recently.


People who commonly receive one include:


- **Landlords:** A business that pays you $2,000 or more in rent in the year, such as a company renting your office space, reports it on a 1099-MISC.
- **Prize and award winners:** Prizes, awards, and other income of $2,000 or more are reported in box 3.
- **Royalty earners:** Royalties of $10 or more are reported in box 2.
- **Health care providers:** Medical and health care payments of $2,000 or more are reported in box 6.
- **Lawyers:** Gross proceeds paid to an attorney of $600 or more are reported in box 10.


The $2,000 threshold is relatively new. For payments made after 31 December 2025, the minimum for most of these categories rose from $600 to $2,000, and it may be adjusted for inflation from 2027. The $10 minimum for royalties and substitute payments, and the $600 minimum for attorney proceeds, did not change. These figures come from the[IRS instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099mec) for 2026 forms, which payers use in early 2027. Backup withholding is reported regardless of the amount.


Payers send their copy to recipients by 31 January. They file with the IRS by 28 February if filing on paper, or 31 March if filing electronically. If a date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next business day. For 2026 payments, since 31 January 2027 falls on a Sunday, the recipient deadline moves to Monday 1 February.


Some payments are reported only if the payer is paying as part of a trade or business, so the rules differ for individuals who pay rent on a home they live in. If you are a payer, check the instructions or ask a tax professional before you file.


*This is general guidance, not professional tax advice. Consult a certified tax professional for your specific situation.*


## 1099-MISC vs 1099-NEC


The difference is simple: the 1099-NEC reports pay for services from someone who is not your employee, and the 1099-MISC reports other payments such as rent, royalties, and prizes. If a business paid you for work you did as a freelancer or contractor, you should get a 1099-NEC, not a 1099-MISC.


1099-NEC 1099-MISC


What it reports Non-employee compensation, which is pay for services Rents, royalties, prizes and awards, medical payments, and other income


Who usually gets one Freelancers, contractors, and self-employed workers Landlords, prize winners, royalty earners, and some service providers


Reporting threshold $2,000 for payments made after December 31, 2025 $2,000 for most categories, $10 for royalties, $600 for attorney proceeds


Recipient copy due January 31 January 31


IRS filing due January 31 February 28 (paper) or March 31 (electronic)


People confuse the two because, before 2020, contractor pay was reported on the 1099-MISC. Many contractors still say they are paid on a "1099-MISC" when they mean the 1099-NEC. If you receive the wrong form, ask the payer to check it, as it affects how the income is reported.

## Frequently asked questions about the 1099-MISC form


### What is a 1099-MISC used for?


A 1099-MISC is used to report miscellaneous income that is not wages or contractor pay, such as rent, royalties, prizes and awards, and certain other payments. The payer files it with the IRS and sends a copy to the recipient.


### What is the difference between 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC?


The 1099-NEC reports pay for services from someone who is not your employee, while the 1099-MISC reports other income such as rent, royalties, and prizes. Contractor pay moved from the 1099-MISC to the 1099-NEC in 2020.


### Is rent reported on a 1099-MISC?


Yes, when a business pays rent of $2,000 or more in a year, it is generally reported in box 1 of the 1099-MISC. The $2,000 threshold applies to payments made after December 31, 2025. It was $600 before that.


### Who files the 1099-MISC?


The payer files it, not the recipient. The payer sends a copy to the recipient by January 31 and files it with the IRS on paper by February 28 or electronically by March 31.


### What if I do not receive my 1099-MISC?


Contact the payer first and ask for the form. You must still report the income on your tax return even if you do not receive one. The[IRS guidance on missing 1099-MISC forms](https://www.irs.gov/faqs/interest-dividends-other-types-of-income/1099-misc-independent-contractors-and-self-employed/1099-misc-independent-contractors-and-self-employed-5) confirms this for prizes and awards.
